questions.title: Bulk invite endpoint that emails from inside a transaction
questions.prompt:
**PR: Add bulk invite endpoint**

> Admins asked to invite a whole team at once. This adds `POST /orgs/:orgId/invites`, which takes a list of emails and a role, creates all the invites in one transaction so a failure leaves nothing behind, and emails each invitee.

Review the change as you would on the real PR. Flag each issue on its line and say how you would fix it.
questions.context:
- Roles are `member`, `admin` and `owner`. The route middleware only checks that the caller belongs to the org (any role).
- `invites` has a unique index on `(org_id, lower(email))` for pending invites.
- The mailer is a third-party HTTP API, p50 about 300 ms.

issues.summary: Unbounded email list processed serially inside one request and one transaction
issues.fix: Cap the batch (for example 100 addresses, 400 with a clear message above that) and validate every address before touching the database. At 300 ms per send, a 1,000-address request holds a transaction open for about 5 minutes and outlives every gateway timeout; large imports should be accepted and processed by a background job.

issues.summary: Role is taken straight from the request body, so any member can create owner invites
issues.fix: Validate `role` against the enum and require the caller's own role to be at least the role granted (only owners invite owners, admins invite admins or members). Enforce it in the service layer, not just the route, since membership is all the middleware proves.

issues.summary: Emails are sent inside the DB transaction: a later failure rolls back invites whose emails already went out
issues.fix: Insert all invites in one statement, commit, and only then send, via an outbox or job queue keyed by invite id so sends retry independently. Rows roll back; delivered emails do not, and holding a transaction across network calls also pins locks and a pool connection.

issues.summary: No normalization or dedupe, so one duplicate or already-invited address aborts the whole batch
issues.fix: Trim and lowercase addresses, dedupe the list, insert with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (or skip existing pending invites), and return per-address results (`created`, `already_invited`, `invalid`) instead of a bare count.

questions.explanation:
The PR's stated safety property, 'a failure leaves nothing behind', is false. The transaction can roll back the rows but not the emails already delivered, so when address 37 hits the unique index (a duplicate in the list, or someone already invited), 36 people hold invite links whose tokens no longer exist, and the client's retry emails them again. That failure is common precisely because nothing normalizes or dedupes the input.

The critical finding is authorization: the middleware proves membership, not privilege, so a `member` can post `role: owner` for an address they control and take over the org. Bounding the batch matters beyond abuse: serial 300 ms sends turn a few hundred addresses into a multi-minute transaction.

The tempting review stops at 'add a limit'. The deeper fix separates the durable write (one transaction, idempotent on `(org, email)`) from side effects (emails after commit, through an outbox).

**Takeaway:** transactions roll back rows, not side effects; anything that leaves the process belongs after the commit.

questions.title: Pricing service that fetches FX rates from its constructor
questions.prompt:
**PR: Add PricingService for multi-currency quotes**

> Quotes catalog prices in the shopper's currency using FX rates from the treasury service. Rates refresh every 5 minutes.

The service is registered as a singleton in the DI container and is also constructed directly in about 40 unit tests. Review the change.

issues.summary: Constructor creates its own HTTP client and starts network I/O, so construction cannot fail cleanly and tests cannot substitute rates
issues.fix: Inject a `RatesSource` interface (the real one wraps the HTTP client) and keep the constructor to field assignment. Do the first load in an explicit `start()` or an async factory that the composition root awaits before marking the pod ready; tests pass a fake source with fixed rates. (The Rust variant even panics when constructed outside a Tokio runtime.)

issues.summary: Missing rate silently falls back to 1.0, so before the first refresh or for an unquoted currency a USD 100 item is quoted as 100 JPY
issues.fix: Treat a missing rate as an error: return or throw `UnsupportedCurrency` / `RatesUnavailable`, refuse quotes until the first successful load, and keep the rates' fetch timestamp so callers can reject stale data.

issues.summary: Background refresh loop started in the constructor has no owner and no way to stop
issues.fix: Give the service a lifecycle (`stop()`, `Dispose`, `AutoCloseable`, a cancellation token or context) or move scheduling to the composition root. Today every test instance leaks a timer or thread, Jest reports open handles, and a second instance doubles the treasury traffic.

issues.summary: Refresh failures are swallowed with no log, metric or staleness bound
issues.fix: Log and count refresh failures, record `lastSuccessAt`, alert when rates are older than an agreed bound (for example 30 minutes), and stop quoting (or flag quotes) past a hard limit so a treasury outage does not silently serve day-old rates.

questions.explanation:
The critical bug is the `1.0` default. In every variant the first load runs in the background, so for the first few hundred milliseconds after start (and forever for any currency treasury does not quote, or after a failed first load) prices are 'converted' at parity: a USD 100 item is offered for 100 JPY. A missing FX rate is an error, never a default.

The design problem underneath is a constructor that does work: it news up its own client, starts I/O and schedules a timer. That is why the 40 unit tests either hit the network or race it, why construction cannot report failure, and why there is no seam to inject fixed rates. Swallowed refresh errors then turn a treasury outage into hours of stale rates with no signal.

Tempting but secondary comments: the hard-coded URL or the 5-minute interval. They are symptoms of the same missing seam.

**Takeaway:** constructors should only assign dependencies; put I/O in an explicit start or factory step that can fail loudly and that tests can replace.

questions.title: Export function with four positional booleans and two callers
questions.prompt:
**PR: Share one export path between the partner feed and the admin download**

> Folds our two export implementations into `exportOrders` so they stop drifting. The nightly job and the admin button now call the same function.

Review the change.
questions.context:
- The partner's SFTP sync picks up every object in `partnerBucket` within about a minute. The partner contract forbids customer PII.
- Support staff use the admin button to pull an org's export while working a ticket.

issues.summary: Four positional booleans make call sites unreadable and transposed arguments invisible to the compiler
issues.fix: Replace the flags with an options object or enums (`{ deleted: 'include', pii: 'redact', compression: 'gzip' }`) and split the function: `buildExport(orgId, spec)` returns bytes, while `publishToPartner(bytes)` and `stageForDownload(bytes)` own the side effects. Each call site then states what it does, and a dry run is simply build without publish.

issues.summary: `dryRun` still uploads the file to the partner bucket; it only skips `markExported`
issues.fix: A dry run must have no external side effects: skip the upload (or write to a scratch prefix the partner never syncs) and return the bytes or a preview. Add a test asserting that no storage write happens in dry-run mode.

issues.summary: Object key always ends in `.csv`, even when the body is gzipped
issues.fix: Derive the extension and Content-Type from the format (`.csv.gz`, `application/gzip`) so the partner's parser and anyone downloading the file handle it correctly; use a run id rather than a millisecond timestamp for uniqueness.

issues.summary: Admin download writes an unredacted, PII-bearing export into the bucket the partner syncs
issues.fix: Never route admin exports through the partner bucket: write them to an internal bucket with short-lived signed URLs, and decide PII inclusion from an explicit, audited permission (for example a `pii:export` grant) instead of hard-coding `true` for all staff.

questions.explanation:
Unifying two callers that sit on different trust boundaries is how this refactor leaks. The admin path inherits the partner path's destination, so every support export, with `includePii = true`, is in the partner's hands a minute later. That is the critical finding, and it is hard to see because `true, false` at a call site reads as noise.

The dry-run flag shows the same smell from another angle: a control flag inside a function with several side effects tends to guard some of them and not others. The `.csv` key on gzipped bytes is a small, real bug of the same kind (the flags interact and nobody checked the combination).

The tempting review is only 'use an options object'. That fixes readability but keeps the coupling. The real fix separates building the export (pure) from publishing it (side effect), so each caller chooses its destination explicitly.

**Takeaway:** when a refactor merges code paths, check that the callers share the same trust boundary and side effects, not just the same steps.

questions.title: Profile PATCH handler that binds the request onto the entity
questions.prompt:
**PR: Let users edit their profile**

> Adds `PATCH /users/:id` so users can change their display name, avatar and timezone. Admins can edit anyone in their org.

This is a multi-tenant SaaS: every user belongs to exactly one org, and `admin` means org admin. Review the change.

issues.summary: Mass assignment: the request body is applied directly to the persistence entity
issues.fix: Bind to a dedicated `UpdateProfileRequest` containing only `displayName`, `avatarUrl` and `timezone`, and copy those fields explicitly. As written a user can send `role: admin`, `emailVerified: true`, a different `orgId`, or even a different `id`, which makes the ORM write over another user's row.

issues.summary: Response serializes the whole entity, including `passwordHash` and `mfaSecret`
issues.fix: Return a `ProfileResponse` built from an allowlist of fields; never serialize persistence entities directly. As defense in depth, mark secret fields as never-serialized (`json:"-"`, `#[serde(skip)]`, `[JsonIgnore]`, `@JsonIgnore`).

issues.summary: Admin check is global, not org-scoped, so any org's admin can edit users in every other org
issues.fix: For the admin path also require `caller.orgId == user.orgId`, ideally by loading the user through an org-scoped query so cross-tenant ids return 404 instead of revealing that the user exists.

issues.summary: No validation of the editable fields
issues.fix: Validate the request type: `timezone` must be a known IANA zone, `displayName` trimmed and length-capped, `avatarUrl` an https URL on the allowed image host; reject unknown fields with a 400 that names them.

questions.explanation:
Binding untrusted input onto an entity is the textbook mass-assignment hole. The endpoint's intent is three fields, but the code accepts every column, so a self-service profile edit becomes privilege escalation (`role`), verification bypass (`emailVerified`) or, with a changed `id`, an overwrite of someone else's row. The response leaks credential material for the mirror-image reason: the entity has become the API contract in both directions.

The tenancy bug is the one reviewers miss, because the authorization check looks complete. `admin` is an org-scoped role being checked as if it were global.

**Takeaway:** give each endpoint its own request and response types, separate from the entity, so the contract is an allowlist a reviewer can read.

questions.title: Trial countdown that reads the wall clock, with a time-bomb test
questions.prompt:
**PR: Add trial countdown banner and paywall**

> Shows a warning during the last 3 days of the 14-day trial and a paywall once it ends. Tests included.

Sales occasionally extends a trial by a week for prospects stuck in procurement. The PR was opened on 2026-11-15 and CI was green. Review the change.

issues.summary: Business logic reads the system clock directly, so it cannot be tested at a chosen instant
issues.fix: Pass `now` in (or inject a `Clock`) and read the real clock once, at the edge in the handler. `trialBanner(account, now)` becomes a pure function you can test at 72 h, 1 h and 0 s before expiry.

issues.summary: Truncating to whole days shows the paywall while up to 23 h 59 m of trial remain
issues.fix: Decide expiry by comparing instants (`now >= trialEndsAt`) and use day counts only for display, rounded up, so the last day reads '1 day left' instead of locking the user out.

issues.summary: Test pins a calendar date while the code reads the real clock, so it passed only on 2026-11-15 and fails from then on
issues.fix: With an injected clock, fix both the trial start and `now` in the test (for example start 2026-11-04T00:00Z, now 2026-11-15T12:00Z) and add boundary cases; never mix absolute fixtures with the real clock.

issues.summary: Trial length is a code constant, so extensions are impossible and changing it silently rewrites every live trial
issues.fix: Store `trialEndsAt` on the account at signup and let Sales move it; derive the banner from that field instead of `trialStartedAt + TRIAL_DAYS`.

questions.explanation:
The test is the giveaway. It fixes a start date and expects '2 days left', which is true for exactly one calendar day of real time (2026-11-15 UTC) because the function consults the wall clock. It was green when the PR was opened and goes red the next morning with no code change, which is how teams learn to ignore failing tests.

The boundary bug comes from deciding with a truncated day count: a user with 20 hours left has `daysLeft = 0` and hits the paywall a day early. Comparing instants for the decision and rounding only for display fixes it, and both cases become trivial to test once `now` is a parameter.

The hard-coded 14 is a modeling gap: the business already extends trials, and a derived end date cannot represent that.

**Takeaway:** time is an input; pass `now` into business logic and test the boundaries explicitly.

questions.title: Ledger retry helper that both loses and duplicates money
questions.prompt:
**PR: Make ledger writes resilient to timeouts**

> The ledger service occasionally times out under load. This adds a generic `retry` helper and wraps the ledger append in `chargeCustomer`. The ledger dedupes appends that share an `idempotencyKey`, so retries are safe.

Review the change.
questions.context: Ledger latency during last week's peak: p50 180 ms, p99 2.1 s. The client timeout for `ledger.append` is 1 s.

issues.summary: A new idempotency key is generated on every attempt, so a retry after a timeout posts a second entry
issues.fix: Derive the key once, outside the retried closure, from the business operation (for example `ledger:charge:<payment.id>`), so every attempt and any later replay dedupes. With a 1 s client timeout against a 2.1 s p99, 'timed out but committed' is the common failure, not an edge case.

issues.summary: Exhausted retries return an empty value and the caller reports success: a captured payment with no ledger entry
issues.fix: Make the helper throw the last error (wrapped with the attempt count) and have `chargeCustomer` fail or hand off to a durable retry (outbox or queue) that guarantees the entry is eventually posted. A warn log is not a recovery mechanism; add a reconciliation alert for payments without ledger entries.

issues.summary: Every error is retried and discarded without logging, including non-retryable ones
issues.fix: Take an `isRetryable(err)` predicate (timeouts, connection resets, 429 and 503), fail fast on validation, auth and programming errors, and log each failed attempt with its error and attempt number. In Java, restore the interrupt flag rather than swallowing `InterruptedException`.

issues.summary: Immediate retries with no backoff, jitter or overall deadline
issues.fix: Back off exponentially with full jitter (for example 100 ms base, 1 s cap) and bound total retry time by the request's deadline, so retries do not pile onto a ledger that is already slow under load.

questions.explanation:
The helper turns one failure mode into two worse ones.

Because the key is minted inside the closure, the ledger's dedupe never fires. An attempt that times out after the ledger committed (likely here: the 1 s client timeout sits below the 2.1 s p99) is followed by an append with a fresh key, and the customer is debited twice. The PR description's claim that 'retries are safe' depends on a key that is stable across attempts, and the code breaks exactly that.

When every attempt fails, the helper converts an error into 'no value' and the caller returns `ok: true` for a payment the ledger has never seen. Money moved at the PSP, the books do not show it, and the only trace is a warn line.

The tempting review is 'add exponential backoff'. That is a real improvement, but minor next to correctness: backoff on a non-idempotent operation just spaces out the duplicates.

**Takeaway:** a retry is only safe when the operation is idempotent across attempts, and a retry helper must surface exhaustion as an error, never as an empty value.

questions.title: Env config loader with silent defaults and lenient parsing
questions.prompt:
**PR: Move service config to environment variables**

> Replaces the hard-coded settings with env vars, with sensible defaults so local dev works with zero setup. Adds the production values file.

Review the loader together with the values file in the context.
questions.context:
```yaml
# deploy/values-prod.yaml (added in this PR)
env:
  PORT: "8080"
  REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS: "30s"
  DB_MAX_CONNECTIONS: "40"
  NEW_CHECKOUT: "true"
  # DATABASE_URL and PAYMENTS_API_KEY are injected by the external-secrets operator
```

issues.summary: Required secrets default silently, so a pod missing DATABASE_URL or PAYMENTS_API_KEY boots against localhost or with an empty key
issues.fix: Treat both as required outside local dev: collect every missing or invalid key and exit at startup with one error listing them, so a broken secret sync fails the rollout at readiness rather than at the first checkout. Keep dev defaults in a `.env.example` or an explicit local profile, not in the production code path.

issues.summary: Malformed numbers are coerced or replaced instead of rejected: REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS=30s becomes 30 ms in TS, no timeout at all in Go, and 30000 elsewhere
issues.fix: Parse strictly (the whole string, digits only, or a duration parser that accepts `30s` on purpose), validate ranges (for example timeout 100 ms to 120 s, pool 1 to 200), and fail startup on invalid input. The loader should return an error, not a `Config` that cannot fail.

issues.summary: Unsafe default direction: a missing APP_ENV turns on error details (stack traces) in production
issues.fix: Fail closed: enable details only when APP_ENV is explicitly `development` (or require APP_ENV everywhere). Security-relevant switches should default to the safe value.

issues.summary: Boolean parsing accepts only "1", so the values file's "true" silently leaves the new checkout off
issues.fix: Parse booleans from an explicit set (`true`, `false`, `1`, `0`, case-insensitive) and reject anything else at startup.

questions.explanation:
Every issue is the same anti-pattern: the loader prefers starting with a guess over failing with a message.

Defaults for required secrets mean a secret-sync outage produces healthy-looking pods pointed at localhost, discovered only when checkout fails. Lenient parsing is worse than it looks and differs by language: TypeScript's `parseInt('30s', 10)` returns 30, so the production timeout becomes 30 ms; Go's ignored `Atoi` error yields 0, which as an `http.Client` timeout means no timeout at all; the Rust, C# and Java variants quietly use 30000 and hide the operator's mistake until someone changes the value and nothing happens. The values file also sets `NEW_CHECKOUT: "true"`, which this loader reads as false, and it never sets APP_ENV, so production serves stack traces.

The tempting position is to bless the defaults because they help local dev. They do, but that convenience belongs in a local profile, not in the code path production runs.

**Takeaway:** parse config strictly and validate it once at startup, failing fast with every problem listed.

questions.title: Offset pagination helper for a live audit log
questions.prompt:
**PR: Add a reusable pagination helper and use it for the audit log**

> Introduces `PageRequest` and `toPage`, and paginates `GET /orgs/:orgId/audit-events`, newest first. Other list endpoints will adopt the helper next.

Review the change.
questions.context:
- `audit_events` holds 40 M rows; the largest org has 6 M.
- Bulk operations write hundreds of events with the same `created_at` millisecond.
- Events keep arriving while admins page through the log.

issues.summary: Offset treats the 1-based page as 0-based, so page 1 skips the newest page of events
issues.fix: Compute `(page - 1) * pageSize` and validate `page >= 1`, or drop page numbers for an opaque cursor. Add a test asserting page 1 returns the newest row.

issues.summary: Ordering by a non-unique timestamp with OFFSET makes pages overlap and skip rows
issues.fix: Add a unique tie-breaker (`ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC`) and, for a live append-heavy table, switch to keyset pagination (`WHERE (created_at, id) < ($ts, $id)`), which stays stable while new events arrive and does not scan the skipped rows.

issues.summary: No bounds on page or pageSize
issues.fix: Clamp `pageSize` to 1..100 and reject non-positive or non-numeric `page` with 400. Guard the multiplication: Rust panics on overflow in debug builds, and Java and C# wrap to a negative offset.

issues.summary: Exact COUNT(*) on every request, and a next-page heuristic that yields a phantom empty last page
issues.fix: Fetch `pageSize + 1` rows to know exactly whether a next page exists, and drop `total` or make it opt-in, cached or estimated: an exact count over 6 M rows on every page view is expensive.

questions.explanation:
The headline bug is plain off-by-one: the API and UI are 1-based (the default is 1), the offset math is 0-based, so the most recent 50 events, the ones an admin opens the audit log to see, never appear. It is critical here because an audit log that silently hides recent activity fails its one job.

The subtler problem is ordering. With hundreds of rows sharing a timestamp, `ORDER BY created_at` gives the database freedom to return ties in any order, so successive pages can repeat and drop rows. Concurrent inserts make OFFSET shift underneath the reader as well. A unique tie-breaker fixes determinism; keyset pagination fixes both, and its cost does not grow with page depth.

Because this is a reusable helper, every endpoint that adopts it inherits these bugs, which is why the review should block now rather than after the second caller.

**Takeaway:** for large, live tables use keyset cursors over a unique sort key; offset pagination is only correct for small, static result sets.

questions.title: In-memory leaderboard mutated by concurrent event handlers
questions.prompt:
**PR: Live leaderboard from score events**

> Keeps per-player totals and a top 10 in memory, updated from `score.awarded` events, and serves `topTen()` to the scoreboard API.

The consumer runs up to 8 handlers concurrently per pod, the broker delivers at least once, and every event carries a unique `eventId`. Review the change.

issues.summary: Read-modify-write of the total is not atomic across concurrent handlers, and the profile call sits between the read and the write
issues.fix: Make the increment atomic and adjacent to the read (`totals.merge(id, points, Long::sum)`, `AddOrUpdate`, or one lock held across read and write) and never await between them. In Go the map is not guarded at all, so concurrent writes crash the process with 'concurrent map writes'.

issues.summary: Not idempotent: at-least-once redelivery double-counts points
issues.fix: Dedupe on `eventId` before applying (a bounded seen-set covering the redelivery window, or persist processed ids with the totals), or change the event to carry the player's new absolute total so applying it twice is harmless.

issues.summary: Top 10 appends an entry per event, so one active player fills several slots with stale scores
issues.fix: Rebuild the top list from `totals` or maintain a structure keyed by player (a sorted set or a map plus heap) so each player appears once, with their current total.

issues.summary: `topTen` hands out the live internal collection that handlers mutate
issues.fix: Return an immutable snapshot: copy under the lock, or build a new immutable list on each update and publish it atomically. Today readers race the writers (Java can throw `ConcurrentModificationException`, Go readers race the in-place sort) and callers can corrupt the board.

issues.summary: A profile-service call on every event couples ingestion throughput to another service
issues.fix: Keep only ids and points on the write path and resolve display names for the ten winners at read time, with a small cache; a slow profile service should not back up the score consumer.

questions.explanation:
Two handlers for the same player both read 100, both await the profile service, then write 100 + their own points; one award vanishes. Concurrent maps do not help: each call is atomic, the sequence is not. In TypeScript the race is just as real because `await` yields between the read and the write, and in Go the unguarded map is a crash, not just a lost update.

Locking fixes atomicity but not duplicates: at-least-once delivery means the same `eventId` will arrive twice after a consumer restart, and an additive handler counts it twice. The top list has its own logic bug, inserting one row per event rather than one per player, and exposing the live list makes every reader a participant in the race.

The tempting single comment is 'add a mutex'. It is necessary, but it leaves the double counting, the duplicate rows and the leaked collection.

**Takeaway:** shared state touched by concurrent, at-least-once handlers needs atomic updates, idempotency and snapshot reads; a lock alone provides only the first.

questions.title: Repository that hands ORM entities and queries to the HTTP layer
questions.prompt:
**PR: Add OrderRepository and the customer order-history endpoint**

> Introduces a repository for orders so handlers stop touching the ORM directly, and wires `GET /me/orders` for the customer app.

Order rows also carry internal columns used by finance and the fraud team. Review the change.

issues.summary: The repository is a pass-through that exposes the ORM's query API, so persistence details leak into handlers
issues.fix: Give it intention-revealing methods, for example `listForCustomer(customerId, cursor): OrderSummary[]`, that own the filter, the item loading and the projection. When callers compose ORM queries, soft-delete filters, tenancy rules and query tuning can no longer be changed in one place, which defeats the PR's own goal.

issues.summary: The handler serializes ORM entities, sending cost, fraud score and internal notes to customers
issues.fix: Map to an explicit `OrderHistoryItem` response with allowlisted fields (id, status, total, placed-at, items with name, quantity and unit price) and add a contract test asserting internal fields never appear in the response.

issues.summary: N+1 queries: one items query or lazy load per order
issues.fix: Load items in one round trip inside the repository, through a join or `WHERE order_id IN (...)` (`relations`, `Preload`, `Include`, a fetch join or `find_with_related`), projected straight into the response type.

issues.summary: Order history is unbounded and unordered
issues.fix: Order by `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` and page with a cursor; long-lived customers and B2B accounts can have thousands of orders.

questions.explanation:
The PR says the repository exists so handlers stop touching the ORM, but the handler still writes ORM queries, just through a thinner wrapper, and receives ORM entities back. That leak is what causes the critical bug: with the entity as the response type, every column is public, so customers receive `costCents` (your margin), `fraudScore` and `internalNotes`. It also hides the N+1: in Java the lazy collection is touched once per order, and Jackson serializing a bidirectional relation can recurse; in Go the per-order association error is silently ignored.

The tempting review is 'add a DTO in the handler'. That fixes the leak in one place, but leaves query composition, item loading and projection scattered across every future caller.

**Takeaway:** a repository earns its keep by hiding persistence, with domain-shaped methods in and domain or read models out; if it returns entities and query builders, the ORM is still your API.

questions.title: Payment webhook with a broken signature check and slow inline work
questions.prompt:
**PR: Handle payment provider webhooks**

> Verifies the provider's signature, marks the order paid, emails the receipt and creates the shipment.

Review the change against the provider's contract in the context.
questions.context:
Provider contract:
- Header `X-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of t + '.' + raw request body>`.
- Deliveries time out after 10 s; any non-2xx or timeout is retried with backoff for 3 days, and endpoints failing for 3 days are disabled.

Receipt PDF rendering takes 2 to 6 s.

issues.summary: Signature is computed over re-serialized JSON instead of the raw body, compared with a non-constant-time equality, and the timestamp is never checked
issues.fix: Read the raw request bytes before any JSON binding and HMAC exactly `t + '.' + raw`; compare with a constant-time function on equal-length bytes (`timingSafeEqual`, `hmac.Equal`, `Mac::verify_slice`, `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`, `MessageDigest.isEqual`); reject timestamps more than 5 minutes from now; accept any of several `v1` values so the secret can rotate.

issues.summary: PDF rendering, email and shipment creation run before the 200, so slow deliveries time out and get retried while still running
issues.fix: Verify, persist the event, and acknowledge with 2xx immediately; do the work in a background worker from the stored event, with each step idempotent and retried independently.

issues.summary: No dedupe on the event id, so retries and replays mark paid, email and ship again
issues.fix: Insert the provider's event id into a `processed_webhook_events` table with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the state change, and skip duplicates; make `createShipment` idempotent on the order id as a second guard.

issues.summary: Unknown event types get a 400, so the provider retries them for 3 days and may disable the endpoint
issues.fix: Return 2xx for event types you do not handle (log them at debug or info), and subscribe only to the types you need.

questions.explanation:
Re-serializing parsed JSON does not reproduce the signed bytes: key order, whitespace, number formatting, escaping and dropped unknown fields all differ. Legitimate deliveries start failing with 401, the provider disables the endpoint after 3 days, and the 'fix' someone ships under pressure is to turn verification off. Even with the right bytes, plain string comparison leaks timing and the unchecked timestamp lets a captured delivery be replayed indefinitely.

Then the handler spends 2 to 6 s rendering a PDF plus two more network calls before acknowledging. Past 10 s the provider times out and redelivers while the first attempt is still running; with no event-id dedupe, each redelivery sends another receipt and creates another shipment. A failure in step three returns 500, and the retry repeats steps one and two.

The tempting review is 'move the work to a queue'. Necessary, but without idempotency on the event id the queue just moves the duplicates downstream.

**Takeaway:** a webhook endpoint should verify the raw bytes, record the event idempotently, acknowledge fast and do the work asynchronously.

questions.title: Single-flight product cache that caches failures forever
questions.prompt:
**PR: Cache product lookups to cut catalog DB load**

> Adds a single-flight read-through cache in front of `getProduct(tenantId, productId)`: concurrent misses share one in-flight load, and price edits invalidate the entry.

Review the change.
questions.context:
- Product ids are per-tenant integer sequences starting at 1; there are about 9,000 tenants.
- The service runs 12 replicas behind a load balancer. Admins edit prices in a separate admin app, which calls `updatePrice` on whichever replica serves the request.
- Checkout reads prices through this cache.

issues.summary: The in-flight future is the cached value, so a failed load is cached forever and one transient DB error poisons that product until restart
issues.fix: On failure, remove the entry, but only if the map still holds that same future so a newer load is not evicted; or keep in-flight loads and completed values in separate maps and always clear the in-flight entry on completion. Go has `golang.org/x/sync/singleflight` for exactly this.

issues.summary: Key concatenation without a delimiter collides across tenants: tenant 1 product 23 and tenant 12 product 3 share key 123
issues.fix: Use a structured key (a tuple or record of tenant id and product id) or a delimiter that cannot occur in either part (`tenantId:productId`), and add a test with colliding pairs. As written, one tenant can be shown, and charged, another tenant's product.

issues.summary: No TTL, size bound or cross-replica invalidation: entries (including not-found results) live forever, and a price edit clears only one of 12 replicas
issues.fix: Use a bounded cache (LRU with a max entry count) with a short TTL plus jitter, broadcast invalidations to all replicas (pub/sub, or a version stamp checked on read), and have checkout price from the source of truth or validate a price version instead of trusting the cache.

issues.summary: Shared loads have no timeout and waiters cannot cancel
issues.fix: Bound the shared load with its own timeout and let each waiter stop waiting on its own context or cancellation token, so one hung query does not stall every request for that product.

questions.explanation:
Single-flight is the right tool for stampedes, but this version caches the future rather than the value, so it also caches failures. One DB timeout during a deploy and that product returns the same error on that replica until the pod restarts; the same applies to a `null` cached for a product looked up moments before it was created.

Because nothing expires, price edits are the next problem: `updatePrice` clears one replica's entry while the other 11 keep serving, and charging, the old price indefinitely. With roughly 9,000 tenants and no bound, memory also grows with every product ever viewed.

The tenant collision is the quiet one. With per-tenant integer ids, string concatenation maps tenant 1/product 23 and tenant 12/product 3 to the same key, a cross-tenant data leak that no single-tenant test will catch.

Language notes: if the Go loader panics before `close`, every waiter blocks forever; Java's `supplyAsync` runs blocking JDBC on the shared ForkJoin pool.

**Takeaway:** a cache is a consistency decision; define structural keys, expiry, cross-replica invalidation and what happens to failures before you add one.
